122.subject: Botany
122.text: The bacteria Pseudomonas aeruginosa is useful because of its ability to
options: transfer genes from one plant to another
decompose a variety of organic compounds
fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil
produce a wide variety of antibiotics.
122.sol:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative, aerobic rod belonging to the bacterial family Pseudomonadaceae. These bacteria are common inhabitants of soil water. They occur regularly on the surfaces of plants and occassionally on the surfaces of animals.
The bacterium will grow in the absence of $\mathrm{O}_2$ if $\mathrm{NO}_3$ is available as a respiratory electron acceptor. $Q, a$ possesses the metabolic versatility. Organic growth factors are not required, and it can use more than thirty organic compounds for growth. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is often observed growing in "distilled water" which is evidence of its minimal nutritional requirements.
- It is able to grow at temperatures as high as 42 degrees.
- Its tolerance to a wide variety of physical conditions, including temperature, contributes to its ecological success and makes it suitable for decomposing a variety of organic compounds in varied environmental conditions.

2007.subject: Zoology
2007.text: Which one of the following four secretions is correctly matched with its source, target and nature of action?
2007.sol:
Gastrin is a polypeptide hormone produced by the enteroendocrine cells of the stomach. It plays an important role in the control of gastric acid secretion. Inhibin hormone is secreted from corpus luteum, placenta and testes. It supplements the effect of excess sex hormones for depressing gonadotrophic activity $(\mathrm{FSH}, \mathrm{LH}, \mathrm{ICSH})$ target of inhibin is anterior lobe of pituitary. Duodenal enterokinase converts trypsinogen to activate trypsin which, in turn, activates the other pancreatic enzymes.
Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) is released by walls of the cardiac atrium in response to high sodium concentration, high extracellular fluid volume, or high blood volume. It then acts via various mechanisms to excrete $\mathrm{Na}$, and to cause vasodilation in the circulatory system. It dilates the afferent glom erular arteriole, constricts the efferent glomerular arteriole, and relaxes the mesangial cells. This increases the glomerular filtration rate, resulting in greater excretion of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$and water. It also decreases Na resorption in the renal distal convoluted tubule and cortical collecting duct. It also inhibits renin secretion.

2084.sol: The blastomeres in the blastocyst are arranged into an outer layer called trophoblast and an inner group of cells attached to trophoblast called the inner cell mass. Inner cell mass looks like a small knob at one pole which gives rise to the embryo and is called the embryonal knob. The trophoblast does not take part in the formation of the embryo proper. It remains external to the embryo and gives rise to the extraembryonic membranes, namely, chorion and amnion, for the protection and nourishment of the embryo. The trophoblast cells in contact with the embryonal knob are known as cells of Rauber.

2097.subject: Zoology
2097.text: Which one of the following is an environmentrelated disorder with the correct main cause ?
options: Black lung disease (pneumoconiosis) found mainly in workers in stone quarries and crushers.
Blue baby disease (methaemoglobinaemia) due to heavy use of nitrogenous fertilizers in the area.
Non-hodgkin's lymphoma found mainly in workers involved in manufacture of neem based pesticides.
Skin cancer mainly in people exposed to benzene and methane.
2097.sol:
Blue baby syndrome is a pathological condition, called methemoglobinemia, in which blood's capacity for oxygen transport is reduced, resulting in bluish skin discoloration in infants. Blue baby syndrome begins when large amounts of nitrates in water are ingested by an infant and converted to nitrite by the digestive system. The nitrite then reacts with oxyhaemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying blood protein) to form metheglobin, which cannot carry oxygen.
Pneumoconiosis is a man-made, occupational lung diseases that are contracted by prolonged breathing of coal mine dust i.e. caused by the inhalation of dust, characterized by formation of nodular fibrotic changes in lungs.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (or NHL) is a cancer of lymphoid tissue, a part of the lymphatic system. NHL is a heterogenous disease.
Skin cancer is a malignant tumor that grows in the skin cells. It is commonly caused by exposure to the sun's UV rays.

5442.subject: Chemistry
5442.text: $300 \mathrm{ mL}$ of a gas ' $x$ ' of molar mass $32 \mathrm{ g} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}$ is effused in 25 seconds. What volume of methane would effuse in the same time?
5442.sol:
Let, the volume of methane effused in $25 \mathrm{ s}$ be $x \mathrm{ mL}$.
Now, from the Graham's law of diffusion,
Rate of effusion $\propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{ Molecular mass }}}$...(i)
Also, rate of effusion $=\frac{\text{ Volume diffused }}{\text{ Time taken }}$...(ii)
From Eq. (i) and (ii) we get,
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{r_x}{r_{\mathrm{CH}_4}}=\sqrt{\frac{M_{\mathrm{CH}_4}}{M_x}} \\ & \frac{\frac{300}{25}}{\frac{x}{25}}=\sqrt{\frac{16}{32}} \Rightarrow \frac{300}{x}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}\Rightarrow \quad x=300 \sqrt{2}=424.26 \mathrm{ mL} \simeq 424 \mathrm{ mL}$

11518.subject: Mathematics
11518.text:
If $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the roots of the equation
$x^2+(\sqrt{3}+2) x+(\sqrt{3}-1)=0,$
then the area of the triangle formed by the lines $y=m_1 x, y=m_2 x$ and $y=c$
11518.sol:
Since, $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the roots of the equation $x^2+(\sqrt{3}+2) x+(\sqrt{3}-1)=0$
then $\quad m_1+m_2=-(\sqrt{3}+2)$,
$m_1 m_2=\sqrt{3}-1$
$\therefore m_1-m_2=\sqrt{\left(m_1+m_2\right)^2-4 m_1 m_2}$
$=\sqrt{(3+4+4 \sqrt{3}-4 \sqrt{3}+4)}$
$=\sqrt{11}$
and coordinates of the vertices of the given triangles are $(0,0),\left(c / m_1, c\right)$ and $\left(c / m_2, c\right)$. Hence, the required area of triangle
$=\frac{1}{2}\left|\begin{array}{ccc}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{c}{m_1} & c & 1 \\ \frac{c}{m_2} & c & 1\end{array}\right|=\frac{1}{2} c^2\left|\left(\frac{1}{m_1}-\frac{1}{m_2}\right)\right|$
$=\frac{1}{2} c^2 \frac{\left|m_2-m_1\right|}{m_1 m_2}$
$=\frac{1}{2} c^2 \frac{\sqrt{11}}{(\sqrt{3}-1)}$
$=\frac{1}{2} c^2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{11} \cdot(\sqrt{3}+1)}{(\sqrt{3}-1)(\sqrt{3}+1)}$
$=\left(\frac{\sqrt{33}+\sqrt{11}}{4}\right) \cdot c^2$

So $\mathrm{a}$ is correct option.

14436.text: An electromagnetic wave of frequency $2 \mathrm{MHz}$ propagates from vacuum to a non-magnetic medium of relative permittivity 9. Then its' wavelength
14436.sol:
In vacuum wavelength,
$\lambda_0=\frac{c}{f_0}=\frac{3 \times 10^8}{2 \times 10^6}=1.5 \times 10^2=150 \mathrm{ m}$
In medium, speed of wave is
$v=\frac{\mathcal{c}}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}} \approx \frac{\mathcal{c}}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}}$
(as medium is non-magnetic)
$\therefore \quad v=\frac{\mathcal{c}}{\sqrt{9}}=\frac{\mathcal{c}}{3}=1 \times 10^8 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$
Frequency remaining same, wavelength in medium is $\lambda=\frac{v}{f_0}=\frac{10^8}{2 \times 10^6}=50 \mathrm{ m}$
$\therefore$ Wavelength decreases by $100 \mathrm{ m}$.

15413.sol:
Let radius of big drop $=R$
Radius of small drop $=r$
Number of small drops, $n=1000$
In this process, the volume remains same
$V_f=V_i\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3=n\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3\right)R^3=1000 r^3 \Rightarrow R=10 r$...(i)
Initial surface area,
$A_1=n 4 \pi r^2$
Final surface area, $A_2=4 \pi R^2$ 
Now, increase in surface area,
$\Delta A=A_2-A_1=4 \pi   \left[R^2-n r²\right]$
We know that, surface energy,
$\mathrm{SE}=\mathrm{TA} [where, $ T=$ surface tension of liquid]
According to question,
\frac{\mathrm{SE}_f}{\mathrm{SE}_i}=\frac{\mathrm{TA}_2}{\mathrm{TA}_1}=\frac{4 \pi R^2}{n\left(4 \pi r^2\right)}=\frac{R^2}{1000 r^2} [$ From Eq. (i)]
$$=\frac{(10 r)^2}{1000 r^2}=\frac{100 r^2}{1000 r^2}=\frac{1}{10}$$ or $1: 10$

19601.subject: Chemistry
19601.text:
Consider the following compounds
ethanamine (i); diethylamine (ii); aniline (iii) and $N$ - methylbenzenamine (iv) The correct decreasing order of pKb values of the compounds is:
19601.sol:
The basicity of amines is inversely proportional to their $pK_b$ values. Higher basicity corresponds to a lower $pK_b$ value.

Comparing the basicity of the given compounds:
1. Diethylamine (ii) is a secondary aliphatic amine. It is the most basic due to the electron-donating inductive effect of two ethyl groups and favorable solvation.
2. Ethanamine (i) is a primary aliphatic amine. It is less basic than diethylamine due to fewer electron-donating groups.
3. $N$-methylbenzenamine (iv) is an aromatic amine where the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalized into the benzene ring, reducing its availability for protonation. However, the methyl group provides a slight electron-donating effect compared to aniline.
4. Aniline (iii) is a primary aromatic amine where the lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring. It is the least basic among the given compounds.

The order of basicity is: (ii) > (i) > (iv) > (iii).

Since $pK_b$ is inversely proportional to basicity, the decreasing order of $pK_b$ values is: (iii) > (iv) > (i) > (ii).

Answer: iii $>$ iv $>$ i $>$ ii

20917.subject: Mathematics
20917.text: A square plate is contracting at a uniform rate of 2 $\text{cm}^2$ / min. The rate at which the perimeter is decreasing when the side of the square is 16 cm is:
20917.sol:
Let $x$ be the side length of the square plate.

Area of the square, $A = x^2$

Perimeter of the square, $P = 4x$

Given that the area is contracting at a uniform rate of $2\ \text{cm}^2/\text\min$, we have:

$\dfrac{dA}{dt} = -2$

Differentiating $A = x^2$ with respect to $t$:

$\dfrac{dA}{dt} = 2x \dfrac{dx}{dt}$

Substituting $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = -2$ and $x = 16$:

$-2 = 2(16) \dfrac{dx}{dt}$

$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\dfrac{1}{16}\ \text{cm}/\text\min$

Now, differentiating $P = 4x$ with respect to $t$:

$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 4 \dfrac{dx}{dt}$

Substituting the value of $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$:

$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 4 \left(-\dfrac{1}{16}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{4}\ \text{cm}/\text\min$

The negative sign indicates that the perimeter is decreasing. Therefore, the rate at which the perimeter is decreasing is $\dfrac{1}{4}\ \text{cm}/\text\min$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4}\ cm\ /\ min$

21290.subject: Mathematics
21290.text: If $\left[\begin{array}{ccc}2+x & 3 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ x & 1 & -5\end{array}$\right]$ is a singular matrix, then $x$ is$
21290.sol:
A matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to zero. Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2+x & 3 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ x & 1 & -5 \end{bmatrix}$.

The determinant $|A|$ is given by:

$|A| = (2+x) \begin{vmatrix} -1 \text{ and } 2 \\ 1 \text{ and } -5 \end{vmatrix} - 3 \begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } 2 \\ x \text{ and } -5 \end{vmatrix} + 4 \begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } -1 \\ x \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Calculating the $2 \times 2$ determinants:

$|A| = (2+x)(5 - 2) - 3(-5 - 2x) + 4(1 - (-x)) = 0$

$|A| = (2+x)(3) - 3(-5 - 2x) + 4(1 + x) = 0$

Expanding the terms:

$6 + 3x + 15 + 6x + 4 + 4x = 0$

Combining like terms:

$13x + 25 = 0$

$13x = -25$

$x = -\dfrac{25}{13}$

Answer: $-\dfrac{25}{13}$

21512.subject: Mathematics
21512.sol:
Let $I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{x + 1}{x(1 + x e^x)} dx$

Multiplying the numerator and the denominator by $e^x$:

$I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{(x + 1)e^x}{x e^x(1 + x e^x)} dx$

Let $x e^x = t$. Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$:

$(x e^x + e^x) dx = dt \Rightarrow (x + 1)e^x dx = dt$

Substituting $t$ and $dt$ into the integral:

$I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{t(1 + t)}$

Using partial fractions:

$I = \displaystyle\int \left( \dfrac{1}{t} - \dfrac{1}{1 + t} \right) dt$

Integrating with respect to $t$:

$I = \log|t| - \log|1 + t| + C$

$I = \log\left|\dfrac{t}{1 + t}\right| + \log|c|$

$I = \log\left|\dfrac{c t}{1 + t}\right|$

Substituting back $t = x e^x$:

$I = \log\left|\dfrac{c x e^x}{1 + x e^x}\right|$

Answer: $\log\left|\dfrac{c x e^x}{1 + x e^x}\right|$

22317.subject: Mathematics
22317.text: $\mathrm{a}=2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \mathrm{b}=\hat{\mathrm{i}}-\hat{\mathrm{j}}$ and $\mathrm{c}=5 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}$, then unit vector parallel to $\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}-\mathrm{c}$ but in opposite direction is
22317.sol:
Given vectors $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$, $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j}$, and $\vec{c} = 5\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

Calculate the vector $\vec{v} = \vec{a} + \vec{b} - \vec{c}$:
$\vec{v} = (2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}) + (\hat{i} - \hat{j}) - (5\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})$
$\vec{v} = (2 + 1 - 5)\hat{i} + (1 - 1 + 1)\hat{j} + (-1 - 0 - 1)\hat{k}$
$\vec{v} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$

The magnitude of $\vec{v}$ is $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (1)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = \sqrt{9} = 3$.

The unit vector in the direction of $\vec{v}$ is $\hat{u} = \dfrac{\vec{v}}{|\vec{v}|} = \dfrac{1}{3}(-2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$.

The unit vector in the opposite direction is $-\hat{u} = -\dfrac{1}{3}(-2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}) = \dfrac{1}{3}(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3}(2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\hat{\mathrm{j}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{k}})$

23197.subject: Physics
23197.text: A particle starts from rest and moves along the x -axis with a velocity that varies as $\mathrm{v}=\sqrt{100+4 x} \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. The acceleration of the particle is:
23197.sol:
Given the velocity $v = \sqrt{100 + 4x}$.

The acceleration $a$ of a particle moving in one dimension is given by $a = v \dfrac{dv}{dx}$.

Differentiating $v = (100 + 4x)^{1/2}$ with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2} (100 + 4x)^{-1/2} \times 4 = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{100 + 4x}}$.

Substituting $v$ and $\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ into the expression for acceleration:

$a = \sqrt{100 + 4x} \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{100 + 4x}}$.

$a = 2 \text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Answer: $2 m s^{-2}$

26361.subject: Physics
26361.text: In an experiment for determination of the focal length of a thin convex lens, the distance of the object from the lens is $10 \pm 0 . 1cm$ and the distance of its real image from the lens is $20 \pm 0 . 2cm$. The error in the determination of focal length of the lens is $n %$. The value of $n$ is _____.
26361.sol:
Given:

Object distance $= 10 \pm 0 . 1cm$

Image distance $= 20 \pm 0 . 2cm$

As per lens formula

$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} . . . \left(i\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{\left(- 10\right)} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$⇒ f = \dfrac{20}{3}cm$

Differentiate equation $\left(i\right)$ on both sides, we get

$\left(- \dfrac{1}{{v}^{2}}\right)dv - \left(\dfrac{- 1}{{u}^{2}}\right)du = \left(\dfrac{- 1}{{f}^{2}}\right)df$

For calculating maximum error, we will add all values

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{{f}^{2}}df = + \dfrac{1}{{v}^{2}}dv + \dfrac{1}{{u}^{2}}du$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{df}{f}\right) \times 100 = \left[\left(\dfrac{0 . 2}{{20}^{2}} + \dfrac{0 . 1}{{10}^{2}}\right)\dfrac{20}{3}\right] \times 100$

$= \left(\dfrac{0 . 2}{4} + \dfrac{0 . 1}{1}\right)\dfrac{20}{3} = 1$

Therefore,

$\dfrac{df}{f} \times 100 = 1 % = n$

26374.subject: Physics
26374.text:
Passage: A container of height $2$ m, length $2$ m and breadth $1$ m is made of insulating vertical walls and two large area horizontal metal plates ($M_1$ and $M_2$) which extend far beyond the vertical walls in all directions. The container is partitioned into two equal chambers with a thin insulating vertical wall. The partition wall contains a small hole of cross-sectional area $\sqrt{10}$ cm$^2$ near its bottom edge. Initially the hole is closed and the left chamber of the container is completely filled with a liquid of dielectric constant $\epsilon_r = 15$ and the right chamber is empty ($\epsilon_r = 1$). At time $t = 0$, the hole is opened and the liquid flows from the left chamber to the right chamber. In both the chambers, the space above the liquid has $\epsilon_r = 1$ and is maintained at atmospheric pressure. The schematic of the container at a time $t > 0$ is shown in the figure.
[Given: acceleration due to gravity is $10$ ms$^{-2}$.]


Question: The height (in m) of the liquid in left chamber at $t = 500$ s is:
26374.sol:
Let $A$ be the cross-sectional area of each chamber and $a$ be the cross-sectional area of the hole.
From the given dimensions, the area of each chamber is $A = 1 \text{ m} \times 1 \text{ m} = 1 \text{ m}^2$.
The area of the hole is $a = \sqrt{10} \text{ cm}^2 = \sqrt{10} \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$.
Let $h_1$ and $h_2$ be the heights of the liquid in the left and right chambers at time $t$, respectively.
By conservation of volume, $A h_1 + A h_2 = A H$, where $H = 2$ m is the initial height of the liquid in the left chamber.
$\Rightarrow h_1 + h_2 = 2$

The velocity of efflux through the hole is given by Torricelli's law:
$v = \sqrt{2g(h_1 - h_2)}$

The rate of flow of the liquid is:
$-A \dfrac{dh_1}{dt} = a \sqrt{2g(h_1 - h_2)}$

Substitute $h_2 = 2 - h_1$ into the equation:
$-A \dfrac{dh_1}{dt} = a \sqrt{2g(2h_1 - 2)}$

Let $y = 2h_1 - 2$. Then $dy = 2 dh_1$, which gives $dh_1 = \dfrac{dy}{2}$.
The differential equation becomes:
$-\dfrac{A}{2} \dfrac{dy}{dt} = a \sqrt{2gy}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{\sqrt{y}} = -\dfrac{2a\sqrt{2g}}{A} dt$

Integrating both sides from $t = 0$ to $t = 500$ s. At $t = 0$, $h_1 = 2$ m, so $y(0) = 2(2) - 2 = 2$ m.
$\int_{2}^{y} y^{-1/2} dy = -\dfrac{2a\sqrt{2g}}{A} \int_{0}^{500} dt$
$[2\sqrt{y}]_{2}^{y} = -\dfrac{2 \times (\sqrt{10} \times 10^{-4}) \times \sqrt{20}}{1} \times 500$
$2\sqrt{y} - 2\sqrt{2} = -1000 \times 10^{-4} \times \sqrt{200}$
$2\sqrt{y} - 2\sqrt{2} = -0.1 \times 10\sqrt{2}$
$2\sqrt{y} - 2\sqrt{2} = -\sqrt{2}$
$2\sqrt{y} = \sqrt{2}$
$\sqrt{y} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

Squaring both sides, we get:
$y = 0.5$

Since $y = 2h_1 - 2$, we have:
$2h_1 - 2 = 0.5$
$2h_1 = 2.5$
$h_1 = 1.25 \text{ m}$

Answer: $1.25$

27775.subject: Chemistry
27775.text:
The linear combination of atomic orbitals to form molecular orbitals takes place only when the combining atomic orbitals

A. have the same energy B. have the minimum overlap C. have same symmetry about the molecular axis D. have different symmetry about the molecular axis

Choose the most appropriate from the options given below:
27775.sol:
The given conditions should be satisfied by atomic orbitals to form molecular orbitals:

(a) The atomic orbital with one electron (completely half filled) can take part in combination or overlapping.

(b) During the time of overlap, the combining orbitals must have opposite spins of electrons.

(c) The combining atomic orbitals must have the same or nearly the same energy. This means that in a homonuclear molecule, the $1$s-atomic orbital of an atom can combine with the $1$s-atomic orbital of another atom, and not with the $2$s-orbital.

(d) The combining atomic orbitals must have proper orientations to ensure that the overlap is maximum.

(e) The extent of overlapping should be large.

The combining atoms should have the same symmetry around the molecular axis for proper combination, otherwise, the electron density will be sparse.

Hence option B is the answer.

Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
27805.sol:
Butan-$1$-ol can undergo hydrogen bonding due to the presence of an $- OH$ group, ethoxyethane (also known as diethyl ether) can also participate in hydrogen bonding.

Even though there are no hydrogen atoms directly bonded to a highly electronegative atom (like$F, O, orN$) in ethoxyethane, the molecule still has polar $C - O$ bonds that can lead to dipole-dipole interactions with other polar molecules.

Owing to intermolecular hydrogen bonding in butanol, it has higher boiling point than ethoxyethane.

29030.text:
Consider $|x|$ is the difference in oxidation states of Mn in highest manganese fluoride and highest manganese oxide. The ions with $|x|$ number of unpaired electrons from the following are:
A. $Sc^{3+}$
B. $Zn^{2+}$
C. $V^{2+}$
D. $Fe^{2+}$
E. $Co^{2+}$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
29030.sol:
The highest manganese fluoride is $MnF_4$, where the oxidation state of Mn is $+4$.

The highest manganese oxide is $Mn_2O_7$, where the oxidation state of Mn is $+7$.

The difference in oxidation states is $|x| = |7 - 4| = 3$.

The number of unpaired electrons in the given ions are:
$Sc^{3+}$: $[Ar] 3d^0 \Rightarrow 0$ unpaired electrons
$Zn^{2+}$: $[Ar] 3d^{10} \Rightarrow 0$ unpaired electrons
$V^{2+}$: $[Ar] 3d^3 \Rightarrow 3$ unpaired electrons
$Fe^{2+}$: $[Ar] 3d^6 \Rightarrow 4$ unpaired electrons
$Co^{2+}$: $[Ar] 3d^7 \Rightarrow 3$ unpaired electrons

Thus, $V^{2+}$ (C) and $Co^{2+}$ (E) have $3$ unpaired electrons.

Answer: C and E Only

30738.text:
Consider the dissociation equilibrium of the following weak acid
$\mathrm{HA} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq})+\mathrm{A}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})$
If the pKa of the acid is 4, then the pH of 10 mMHA solution is $\_\_\_\_$.(Nearest integer)
[Given: The degree of dissociation can be neglected with respect to unity]
30738.sol:
For the weak acid dissociation $HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$ with pKa = 4
We have Ka = 10⁻⁴.
For a 10 mM (0.01 M) solution where the degree of dissociation is negligible with respect to unity, the concentration of HA remains approximately 0.01 M.
The equilibrium expression gives
$Ka = \frac{[H^+]^2}{[HA]}$
Substituting: $10^{-4} = \frac{[H^+]^2}{0.01}$, which yields $[H^+]^2 = 10^{-6}$, so $[H^+] = 10^{-3}$ M.
Therefore, pH = $-\log(10^{-3}) = 3$.

32247.text: Which transition in the hydrogen spectrum would have the same wavelength as the Balmer type transition from $n = 4$ to $n = 2$ of ${He}^{+}$spectrum
32247.sol:
For ${He}^{+}$ ion, the wave number associated with the Balmer transition, $n = 4$ to $n = 2$ is given by:

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = {RZ}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{{n}_{1}}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{{n}_{2}}^{2}}\right)$

Where, ${n}_{1} = 2$

${n}_{2} = 4$

$Z$ = atomic number of helium

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R ( 2{)}^{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{{2}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{4}^{2}}\right]$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 4R\left[\dfrac{4 - 1}{16}\right]$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3R}{4}$

$⇒ \lambda = \dfrac{4}{3R}$

According to the question, the desired transition for hydrogen will have the same wavelength as that of ${He}^{+}$.

$\lambda ( H ) = \lambda\left({He}^{+}\right)$

$R ( 1{)}^{2}\left[1{n}_{1}^{2} - 1{n}_{2}^{2}\right] = \dfrac{3R}{4}$

By hit and trial method,

$1{n}_{1}^{2} - 1{n}_{2}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{{1}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{2}^{2}}$

On comparing ${n}_{1} = 1 \text{ and } {n}_{2} = 2$

So, the correct answer is n = 2 to n = 1.

33902.text: If z and $\omega$ are two complex numbers such that $\left|z\omega\right| = 1$ and $arg\left(z\right) - arg( \omega ) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, then:
33902.sol:
Let $\left|z\right| = r$ and $arg\left(z\right) = \theta,$ given $arg\left(z\right) - arg\left(\omega\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$⇒ \theta - arg\left(\omega\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$⇒ arg\left(\omega\right) = \theta - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

We know that, if $\left|z\right| = r \text{$ and $} arg\left(z\right) = \theta$ then $\dfrac{1}{\left|z\right|} = \dfrac{1}{r} \text{$ and $} arg\left(\overset{¯}{z}\right) = - arg\left(z\right) = - \theta,$

Hence, $\left|\omega\right| = \dfrac{1}{r}$ and $arg( \overset{¯}{\omega} ) = - arg\left(\omega\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta$

Now, by using Euler form i.e. if $\left|z\right| = r \text{$ and $} arg\left(z\right) = \theta,$ then $z = r{e}^{i\theta},$ we have $z = r{e}^{i\theta}$ and $\omega = \dfrac{1}{r}{e}^{i ( \theta - \dfrac{\pi}{2} )}$

Also, $\overset{¯}{z}\omega = r{e}^{- i\theta} \times \left(\dfrac{1}{r}{e}^{i\left(\theta - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}\right)$

$⇒ \overset{¯}{z}\omega = {e}^{- i\dfrac{\pi}{2}}$

Using polar form i.e. ${e}^{i\theta} = cos\theta + isin\theta,$ we get

$\overset{¯}{z}\omega = 1\left[cos\left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + isin\left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right] = - i$

$⇒ \overset{¯}{z}\omega = - i .

$

34253.text: Let $f$ be a differentiable function satisfying $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}{∫}_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}f\left(\dfrac{{\lambda}^{2}x}{3}\right)d\lambda, x > 0$ and $f\left(1\right) = \sqrt{3}$. If $y = f\left(x\right)$ passes through the point $\left(\alpha, 6\right)$, then $\alpha$ is equal to _______.
34253.sol:
Given,

$f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}{∫}_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}f\left(\dfrac{{\lambda}^{2}x}{3}\right)d\lambda$

Now let $\dfrac{{\lambda}^{2}x}{3} = t$

$⇒ \dfrac{2\lambdax}{3}d\lambda = dt$

$⇒ d\lambda = \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1\sqrt{x}}{x \cdot \sqrt{3}\sqrt{t}}dt$

$⇒ d\lambda = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \cdot \dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{t}}$

So, $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}{∫}_{0}^{x}\dfrac{f\left(t\right)}{\sqrt{t}}dt$

$\sqrt{x}f\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{x}\dfrac{f\left(t\right)}{\sqrt{t}}dt$

Now differentiating both side we get,

$⇒ \sqrt{x} \cdot {f}^{'}\left(x\right) + \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{2\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{\sqrt{x}}$

$⇒ \sqrt{x} \cdot {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{2\sqrt{x}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{y} = \dfrac{dx}{2x}$

Now integrating both side we get,

$⇒ ∫ \dfrac{dy}{y} = ∫ \dfrac{dx}{2x}$

$⇒ lny = \dfrac{1}{2}lnx + lnc$

Given $f\left(1\right) = \sqrt{3}$, so $⇒ ln\sqrt{3} = 0 + lnc$

$⇒ c = \sqrt{3}$

So, $f\left(x\right) = \sqrt{3x}$

Now given $f\left(x\right)$ is passing through $\left(\alpha, 6\right)$,

So $f\left(\alpha\right) = 6 ⇒ 36 = 3\alpha$

$⇒ \alpha = 12$

36176.text: Let chord PQ of length $3\sqrt{13}$ of the parabola $y^2 = 12x$ be such that the ordinates of points $P$ and $Q$ are in the ratio $1:2$. If the chord PQ subtends an angle $\alpha$ at the focus of the parabola, then $\sin\alpha$ is equal to:
36176.sol:
Let the coordinates of points $P and Q$ on the parabola $y^2 = 12x$ be $(x_1, y_1) and (x_2, y_2)$.

Given that the ordinates are in the ratio $1:2$, we have $y_2 = 2y_1$.

Since $P and Q$ lie on the parabola, their abscissae are $x_1 = \dfrac{y_1^2}{12}$ and $x_2 = \dfrac{y_2^2}{12} = \dfrac{4y_1^2}{12} = \dfrac{y_1^2}{3}$.

The length of the chord $PQ$ is $3\sqrt{13}$, so $PQ^2 = 117$.

Using the distance formula:

$(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 = 117$

$\left(\dfrac{y_1^2}{3} - \dfrac{y_1^2}{12}\right)^2 + (2y_1 - y_1)^2 = 117$

$\left(\dfrac{y_1^2}{4}\right)^2 + y_1^2 = 117$

$\dfrac{y_1^4}{16} + y_1^2 - 117 = 0$

$y_1^4 + 16y_1^2 - 1872 = 0$

$(y_1^2 + 52)(y_1^2 - 36) = 0$

Since $y_1^2 > 0$, we get $y_1^2 = 36$, which gives $y_1 = 6$ (taking the positive root by symmetry).

Substituting $y_1 = 6$, we get $x_1 = \dfrac{36}{12} = 3$. Thus, $P$ is $(3, 6)$.

For $Q$, y_2 = 12 and $x_2 = \dfrac{144}{12} = 12$. Thus, $Q$ is $(12, 12)$.

The focus of the parabola $y^2 = 12x$ is $S(3, 0)$.

The vectors from the focus $S$ to points $P and Q$ are:

$\overrightarrow{SP} = (3 - 3)\hat{i} + (6 - 0)\hat{j} = 6\hat{j}$

$\overrightarrow{SQ} = (12 - 3)\hat{i} + (12 - 0)\hat{j} = 9\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$

The angle $\alpha$ subtended by $PQ$ at the focus is the angle between $\overrightarrow{SP} and \overrightarrow{SQ}$.

$\cos\alpha = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{SP} \cdot \overrightarrow{SQ}}{|\overrightarrow{SP}| |\overrightarrow{SQ}|}$

$\cos\alpha = \dfrac{0(9) + 6(12)}{6 \times \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2}} = \dfrac{72}{6 \times 15} = \dfrac{72}{90} = \dfrac{4}{5}$

Therefore, $\sin\alpha = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2\alpha} = \sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^2} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{5}$

Also we know that variance $\left({\sigma}^{2}\right) = \dfrac{∑ {f}_{i}{\left(\overset{¯}{x} - {x}_{i}\right)}^{2}}{∑ {f}_{i}}$

${\sigma}^{2} = \dfrac{2 \times {\left(28 - 5\right)}^{2} + 3 \times {\left(28 - 15\right)}^{2} + 6 \times {\left(28 - 25\right)}^{2} + 5 \times {\left(28 - 35\right)}^{2} + 4 \times {\left(28 - 45\right)}^{2}}{20}$

${\sigma}^{2} = 151$

37716.text: Let $\left(5, \dfrac{a}{4}\right)$, be the circumcenter of a triangle with vertices A ( a, - 2 ) , B ( a, 6 ) and C $\left(\dfrac{a}{4}, - 2\right)$. 37716.sol:
Given: $A\left(a, - 2\right), B\left(a, 6\right)\text{and}C\left(\dfrac{a}{4}, - 2\right)$

$⇒ A{B}^{2} = {\left(a - a\right)}^{2} + {\left(6 + 2\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ A{B}^{2} = 64 . . . \left(i\right)$

$⇒ B{C}^{2} = {\left(a - \dfrac{a}{4}\right)}^{2} + {\left(6 + 2\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ B{C}^{2} = \dfrac{9{a}^{2}}{16} + 64 . . . \left(ii\right)$

$⇒ A{C}^{2} = {\left(a - \dfrac{a}{4}\right)}^{2} + {\left(- 2 + 2\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ A{C}^{2} = \dfrac{9{a}^{2}}{16} . . . \left(iii\right)$

Using $\left(i\right), \left(ii\right)\text{and}\left(iii\right)$,

$⇒ A{C}^{2} + A{B}^{2} = B{C}^{2}$

So, $△ ABC$ is right angled at $A$.

So, circumcentre will be mid-point of $BC$.

$⇒ S ≡ \left(\dfrac{a + \dfrac{a}{4}}{2}, \dfrac{6 - 2}{2}\right)$

$⇒ S ≡ \left(\dfrac{5a}{8}, 2\right) = \left(5, \dfrac{a}{4}\right)$

$⇒ a = 8$

$⇒ BC = \sqrt{\dfrac{9 \times 64}{16} + 64}$

$⇒ BC = \sqrt{100} = 10$

$⇒ AB = 8$

$⇒ AC = \sqrt{\dfrac{9 \times 64}{16}}$

$⇒ AC = 6$

Now, circumradius is given by,

$R = \dfrac{BC}{2} = 5 ⇒ \alpha = 5$

Now, area of triangle will be $\beta = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 8 = 24$ and perimeter will be $\gamma = 6 + 8 + 10 = 24$

38128.text: Consider the line $L$ given by the equation $\dfrac{x - 3}{2} = \dfrac{y - 1}{1} = \dfrac{z - 2}{1} .$ Let $Q$ be the mirror image of the point $( 2, 3, - 1 )$ with respect to $L .$ Let a plane $P$ be such that it passes through $Q,$ and the line $L$ is perpendicular to $P .$ Then which of the following points is on the plane $P ?$
38128.sol:
We have,

$L: \dfrac{x - 3}{2} = \dfrac{y - 1}{1} = \dfrac{z - 2}{1} = k$

Let $R ≡ \left(2, 3, - 1\right)$ and $Q ≡\left(a, b, c\right)$

And, $M ≡ \left(2k + 3, k + 1, k + 2\right).

Direction ratios$ of RM$ is \left(2k + 1, k - 2, k + 3\right),

Then, $RM ⊥ L$, therefore

$2$\left(2k + 1\right)$ + $\left(k - 2\right)$ + $\left(k + 3\right)$ = 0$

$⇒ 6k = - 3$

$⇒ k = - $\dfrac{1}{2}.

$M ≡ $\left(2, \dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{3}{2}$\right)$

Let $Q ≡ $\left(a, b, c\right)$

Also, mid-point of $RQ$ is $M$,

$\dfrac{a + 2}{2} =$2 ⇒ a = 2$

\dfrac{b + 3}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ b = - 2$

$\dfrac{c - 1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}$ ⇒ c = 4$

Hence, $Q ≡ $\left(2, - 2, 4\right)$.

Plane $P$ is perpendicular to line

$\dfrac{x - 3}{2} = \dfrac{y - 1}{1} = \dfrac{z - 2}{1}

and passes through $Q$\left(2, - 2, 4\right)$, therefore equation of plane $P$ is

$2 ( x - 2 ) + 1 ( y + 2 ) + 1 ( z - 4 ) = 0$

$⇒ 2x + y + z - 6 = 0$

Point $\left(1, 2, 2\right)$ satisfies above equation.

40435.subject: Physics
40435.text: A particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ is projected from origin with an initial velocity $\vec{v} = \left(\dfrac{v_0}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{x} + \dfrac{v_0}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{y}\right)$. There exists a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B} = B_0 \hat{z}$ and a space varying electric field $\vec{E} = E_0 e^{-\lambda x}\hat{x}$ within the region $0 \leq x \leq L$. After travelling a distance such that $x$-coordinate has changed from $x=0$ to $x=L$, the change in the kinetic energy is _______.
40435.sol:
According to the work-energy theorem, the change in kinetic energy of a particle is equal to the total work done by all the forces acting on it.

The forces acting on the particle are the electric force and the magnetic force. The magnetic force is given by $\vec{F}_B = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$. Since the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity vector of the particle, the work done by the magnetic field is zero.

The change in kinetic energy is equal to the work done by the electric field alone. The electric force is $\vec{F}_E = q\vec{E} = qE_0 e^{-\lambda x}\hat{x}$.

The work done by the electric field as the particle moves from $x = 0$ to $x = L$ is given by

$W_E = \int_{0}^{L} \vec{F}_E \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_{0}^{L} qE_0 e^{-\lambda x} dx$

Evaluating the integral, we get

$W_E = qE_0 \left[ \dfrac{e^{-\lambda x}}{-\lambda} \right]_{0}^{L}$

$W_E = -\dfrac{qE_0}{\lambda} (e^{-\lambda L} - e^{0})$

$W_E = \dfrac{qE_0}{\lambda} [1 - e^{-\lambda L}]$

Thus, the change in kinetic energy is $\dfrac{qE_0}{\lambda} [1 - e^{-\lambda L}]$.

Answer: $\dfrac{qE_0}{\lambda}[1 - e^{-\lambda L}]$

40897.text:
A body is projected vertically upwards from the surface of earth with a velocity equal to one third of escape velocity. The maximum height attained by the body will be
(Take radius of earth $= 6400km$ and $g = 10{ms}^{- 2}$)
40897.sol:
Total mechanical energy of the body at the surface of earth

${M}_{i} = - \dfrac{GMm}{R} + \dfrac{1}{2}m{\left[\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\right)\right]}^{2} = - \dfrac{GMm}{R} + \dfrac{GMm}{9R} = - \dfrac{8GMm}{9R}$

Total mechanical energy of the body at the highest point

${M}_{f} = - \dfrac{GMm}{R + h}$

Using conservation of mechanical energy,

${M}_{i} = {M}_{f} ⇒ - \dfrac{GMm}{R + h} = - \dfrac{8GMm}{9R}$

$⇒ R + h = \dfrac{9R}{8}$

$⇒ h = \dfrac{R}{8} = \dfrac{6400}{8} = 800km$

41410.subject: Physics
41410.text: $1\,\mu$C charge moving with velocity $\vec{v} = \left(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\right)$ m/s in the region of magnetic field $\vec{B} = \left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\right)$ T. The magnitude of force acting on it is $\sqrt{\alpha} \times 10^{-6}$ N. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
41410.sol:
The magnetic force acting on a moving charge is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

Given:
$q = 1 \, \mu\text{C} = 10^{-6} \text{ C}$
$\vec{v} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$
$\vec{B} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$

Calculating the cross product $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$:
$\vec{v} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & -5 \end{vmatrix}$

$\vec{v} \times \vec{B} = \hat{i}(10 - 9) - \hat{j}(-5 - 6) + \hat{k}(3 + 4)$
$\vec{v} \times \vec{B} = \hat{i} + 11\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}$

The magnitude of $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$ is:
$|\vec{v} \times \vec{B}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 11^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{1 + 121 + 49} = \sqrt{171}$

The magnitude of the force is:
$|\vec{F}| = q |\vec{v} \times \vec{B}| = 10^{-6} \times \sqrt{171} = \sqrt{171} \times 10^{-6} \text{ N}$

Comparing this with the given expression $\sqrt{\alpha} \times 10^{-6} \text{ N}$, we get:
$\alpha = 171$

Answer: $171$

41803.text: In an experiment of determine the Young's modulus of wire of a length exactly $1m$, the extension in the length of the wire is measured as $0 . 4mm$ with an uncertainty of $\pm 0 . 02mm$ when a load of $1kg$ is applied. The diameter of the wire is measured as $0 . 4mm$ with an uncertainty of $\pm 0 . 01mm$. The error in the measurement of Young's modulus $\left(\DeltaY\right)$ is found to be $x \times {10}^{10}N{m}^{- 2}$. The value of $x$ is _____ .
41803.sol:
Given here,

Length, $L = 1m$ and extension in length, $\DeltaL = 0 . 4 \times {10}^{- 3}m$

Mass of load, $m = 1kg$ and diameter of wire, $d = 0 . 4 \times {10}^{- 3}m$

Young's modulus is given by

$Y = \dfrac{FL}{A\DeltaL} = \dfrac{\left(mg\right) \times \left(1\right)}{\left(\dfrac{\pi{d}^{2}}{4}\right)0 . 4 \times {10}^{- 3}}$

$⇒ Y = \dfrac{10 \times 4}{\pi{\left(0 . 4 \times {10}^{- 3}\right)}^{2} \times 0 . 4 \times {10}^{- 3}}$

$⇒ Y = \dfrac{40 \times 7}{22 \times 64 \times {10}^{- 3} \times {10}^{- 9}}$

$⇒ Y = 0 . 199 \times {10}^{- 12}N{m}^{- 2}$

Error in measurement of Young's modulus,

$\dfrac{\DeltaY}{Y} = \dfrac{\DeltaF}{F} + \dfrac{\DeltaL}{L} + \dfrac{\DeltaA}{A} + \dfrac{\Delta\left(\DeltaL\right)}{\left(\DeltaL\right)}$

$= \dfrac{0 . 02}{0 . 4} + 2\dfrac{\Deltad}{d} = \dfrac{0 . 2}{4} + 2 \times \dfrac{0 . 01}{0 . 4}$

$= \dfrac{0 . 1}{2} + \dfrac{0 . 1}{2} = 0 . 1$

$= 0 . 199 \times {10}^{11} \approx 2 \times {10}^{10}$

Hence, the value of $x = 2$.

42232.text: A ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of $150m{s}^{- 1}$. The ratio of velocity after $3s$ and $5s$ is $\dfrac{x + 1}{x}$. The value of $x$ is _____. {take, $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$}
42232.sol:
The formula to calculate the velocity of the ball after $3s$ is given by

${v}_{3} = u - 3g . . . \left(1\right)$

The formula to calculate the velocity of the ball after $5s$ is given by

${v}_{5} = u - 5g . . . \left(2\right)$

Divide equation (1) by equation (2) to obtain the required ratio.

$\dfrac{{v}_{3}}{{v}_{5}} = \dfrac{u - 3g}{u - 5g} . . . \left(3\right)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (3) to calculate the required ratio.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{{v}_{3}}{{v}_{5}} & = & \dfrac{150 - 30}{150 - 50} \\ & = & \dfrac{120}{100} \\ & = & \dfrac{6}{5} \\ & = & \dfrac{5 + 1}{5}\end{cases}$

Comparing the above equation with the given expression, it can be written that $x = 5$.

43226.subject: Physics
43226.text: For rolling spherical shell, the ratio of rotational kinetic energy and total kinetic energy is $\dfrac{x}{5}$. The value of $x$ is _____.
43226.sol:
The rotational kinetic energy is given by

${K}_{rot} = \dfrac{I{\omega}^{2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{3}M{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2}$.

The total kinetic energy is given by

${K}_{tot} = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{3}M{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2} = \dfrac{m{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3}M{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2} = \dfrac{5}{6}M{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2}$

Thus, the ratio is

$\dfrac{{K}_{rot}}{{K}_{tot}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{3}M{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2}}{\dfrac{5}{6}M{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2}} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

Comparing with the given value,

$\dfrac{x}{5} = \dfrac{2}{5} ⇒ x = 2$

- One megaspore divides meiotically to form four megaspores.
- Sometimes meiotic division of the megaspore mother cell is not accompanied by cytokinesis and hence all the four haploid nuclei lie in a single cell called coeno-megaspore.
- All the four nuclei of coeno-megaspore participate in the formation of the embryo sac.
- This type of embryo sac is called as tetrasporic like in Peperomia.
- The four haploid nuclei of coeno-megaspore undergo two successive mitotic divisions forming 16 nuclei.

46560.subject: Physics
46560.text: A short linear object of length $b$ lies along the axis of a concave mirror of focal length $f$ at a distance $u$ from the pole of the mirror, what is the size of image?
46560.sol:
Using the relation for the focal length of concave mirror
$\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}$ ...(1)
Differentiating equation (1), we obtain
$0=-\frac{1}{v^2} d v-\frac{1}{u^2} d u$
So, $\quad d v=-\frac{v^2}{u^2} \times b \ldots(2)$
(Here : $d u=b$ )
From equation (1)
$\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{v} & =\frac{1}{f}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{u-f}{f u} \\
\frac{u}{v} & =\frac{u-f}{f} \\
\end{aligned} \frac{v}{u}=\frac{f}{u-f} \ldots(3)$
Now, from equations (2) and (3), we get
$d v=-\left(\frac{f}{u-f}\right)^2 b$
Therefore, size or image is $=\left(\frac{f}{u-f}\right)^2 b$

46659.text: In Carnot engine efficiency is $40 \%$ at hot reservoir temperature $T$. For efficiency $50 \%$, what will be temperature of hot reservoir?
46659.sol:
The efficiency of a heat engine is defined as the ratio of work done to the heat supplied, ie,
$\eta=\frac{\text{ Work done }}{\text{ Heat input }}=\frac{W}{Q}$
or $\quad \eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}$
where $T_2$ is temperature of sink, and $T_1$ is temperature of hot reservoir
$\therefore \quad \frac{40}{100}=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{T_2}{T_1}=0.6 \Rightarrow \quad T_1=0.6 T_1$
Again, $\quad \frac{50}{100}=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1^{\prime \prime}} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{T_2}{T_1{ }^{\prime}}=0.5 \begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \frac{0.6 T_1}{T_1{ }^{\prime}}=0.5 \\ \therefore & T_1{ }^{\prime}=\frac{0.6}{0.5} T_1=\frac{6}{5} T\end{array}$

51057.text: The ionic radii of ${Na}^{+}, F^{-}, O^{2 -}, N^{3 -}$ follow the order
51057.sol:
The given species are isoelectronic (same number of electrons) to each other. In case of isoelectronic species, cation with greater positive charge will have a smaller radius because of the greater attraction of the electrons to nucleus. Anion with greater negative charge will have the largest radius. This is because the net repulsion of electrons will out weight the nuclear charge and the ion will expand in size. Thus, the order of ionic radii will be,

$N^{3 -} > O^{2 -} > F^{-} > {Na}^{+}$

56846.text: What product is obtained by electrolysis of $50 \%$ solution of sulfuric acid on further hydrolysis?
56846.sol:
Electrolysis of a $50\%$ sulfuric acid solution produces peroxodisulfuric acid (H_2S_2O_8$) at the anode through the oxidation reaction: 2SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow S_2O_8^{2-} + 2e^-$, followed by protonation: $S_2O_8^{2-} + 2H^+ \rightarrow H_2S_2O_8$.

Hydrolysis of $H_2S_2O_8$ proceeds via two steps: initial conversion to peroxymonosulfuric acid (H_2SO_5$) with $H_2S_2O_8 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_5 + H_2SO_4$, followed by decomposition to hydrogen peroxide with $H_2SO_5 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_4 + H_2O_2$.

The final product is therefore hydrogen peroxide (H_2O_2$), corresponding to option \boxed{D}$.

56858.subject: Chemistry
56858.text:
If $E^{{}^{\circ}}\left(\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})}\right)=-0 \cdot 76 \mathrm{ V}$.
Calculate potential for $\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}_{(0.01 \mathrm{M})}^{+2}+2 \overline{\mathrm{e}}$ at 298 K ?
56858.sol:
The standard oxidation potential is the negative of the standard reduction potential: $E^{}^{\circ}_{\text{ox}} = -(-0.76\ \mathrm{V}) = +0.76\ \mathrm{V}$.

The Nernst equation for oxidation at $T = 298\ \mathrm{K}$ is $E = E^{}^{\circ}_{\text{ox}} - \frac{0.0592}{n} \log Q$, where $n = 2$ and $Q = [\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}] = 0.01$.

Substituting these values:

$E = 0.76 - \frac{0.0592}{2} \log(10^{-2})$

Since $\log(10^{-2}) = -2$, the result is $E = 0.76 + 0.0592 = 0.8192\ \mathrm{V}$.

Final potential: $+0.8192\ \mathrm{V}$

56875.subject: Chemistry
56875.text:
If $\mathrm{E}^{{}^{\circ}}\left(\mathrm{Mg}^{+2}{ }_{(\mathrm{aq})} \mid \mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})}\right)=-2.37 \mathrm{ V}$.
What is potential for $\mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{+2}(0.1 \mathrm{M})+2 \overline{\mathrm{e}}$ at 298 K ?
56875.sol:
The standard oxidation potential $E^{}^{\circ}_\text{ox}$ is determined from the given reduction potential $E^{}^{\circ}(\mathrm{Mg}^{+2}_{(\mathrm{aq})} \mid \mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})}) = -2.37\,\mathrm{V}$:

$E^{}^{\circ}_\text{ox} = -E^{}^{\circ}_\text{red} = +2.37\,\mathrm{V}$

For the reaction $\mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})} \to \mathrm{Mg}^{+2}(0.1\,\mathrm{M}) + 2e^-$, the number of electrons transferred is $n = 2$ and the reaction quotient is $Q = [\mathrm{Mg}^{+2}] = 0.1$.

The Nernst equation gives the oxidation potential as:

$E = E^{}^{\circ}_\text{ox} - \frac{0.0592}{n} \log Q = 2.37 - \frac{0.0592}{2} \log(0.1)$

Since $\log(0.1) = -1$, the calculation becomes:

$E = 2.37 - 0.0296 \times (-1) = 2.37 + 0.0296 = 2.3996\,\mathrm{V}$

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

58233.subject: Chemistry
58233.text: What is oxidation state of xenon in xenonmonooxytetrafluoride?
58233.sol:
The oxidation state of xenon in xenonmonooxytetrafluoride (XeOF_4$) is determined by considering the known oxidation states of oxygen and fluorine. Oxygen typically has an oxidation state of $-2$, and fluorine is always $-1$ in compounds. Since $XeOF_4$ is neutral, the sum of the oxidation states is zero.

Let $x$ be the oxidation state of xenon. The equation becomes:

$x + (-2) + 4(-1) = 0$

Simplifying: $x - 2 - 4 = 0$

Thus, $x - 6 = 0$ and $x = +6$.

The oxidation state of xenon is +6, corresponding to answer choice C.

59915.subject: Chemistry
59915.text: Identify from following the correct set of thermodynamic conditions for the reaction to be nonspontaneous at all temperature.
59915.sol:
Spontaneity is determined by the Gibbs free energy change:

$\Delta G = \Delta H - T \Delta S$

For a reaction to be nonspontaneous at all temperatures, $\Delta G > 0$ must hold regardless of $T$.

A reaction with $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$ gives $\Delta G = \text{positive} - T(\text{negative}) = \text{positive} + T(\text{positive})$.
Since both terms are positive, $\Delta G > 0$ for all $T$, ensuring nonspontaneity.

Other combinations depend on temperature: $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$ can be spontaneous at low $T$, $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$ can be spontaneous at high $T$, and $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$ is always spontaneous.

Final answer: $\boxed{D}$

60206.subject: Mathematics
60206.text: The equation of tangent to the curves $x = 1 - 3t^2$ and $y = t - 3t^3$ at the point $(-2,2)$ is...
60206.sol:
Given $x = 1 - 3t^2$ and $y = t - 3t^3$.

At the point $(-2, 2)$, we have $1 - 3t^2 = -2 \Rightarrow 3t^2 = 3 \Rightarrow t = \pm 1$.

Also $t - 3t^3 = 2$. For $t = -1$, $-1 - 3(-1)^3 = 2$, which satisfies the equation. Thus, $t = -1$.

Differentiating $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t$:

$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -6t$

$\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 1 - 9t^2$

The slope of the tangent is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}} = \dfrac{1 - 9t^2}{-6t}$.

At $t = -1$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1 - 9(-1)^2}{-6(-1)} = \dfrac{-8}{6} = -\dfrac{4}{3}$.

The equation of the tangent at $(-2, 2)$ is:

$y - 2 = -\dfrac{4}{3}(x - (-2))$

$3(y - 2) = -4(x + 2)$

$3y - 6 = -4x - 8$

$4x + 3y + 2 = 0$

Answer: $4x + 3y + 2 = 0$

61235.text: The lines $x+2 a y+a=0, x+3 b y+b=0, x+4 c y+c=0$ are concurrent then $a, \mathrm{ b}, \mathrm{c}$ are in
61235.sol:
The concurrency of lines $x + 2ay + a = 0$, $x + 3by + b = 0$, and $x + 4cy + c = 0$ requires the determinant of their coefficients to vanish:

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 \text{ and } 2a \text{ and } a \\ 1 \text{ and } 3b \text{ and } b \\ 1 \text{ and } 4c \text{ and } c \end{vmatrix} = 0.$

Expanding this determinant yields $ -bc + 2ac - ab = 0 $. For nonzero $a$, $b$, and $c$, dividing by $abc$ gives

$ -\frac{1}{a} + \frac{2}{b} - \frac{1}{c} = 0, $

which simplifies to $ \frac{2}{b} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{c} $. This is the condition for $ \frac{1}{a}, \frac{1}{b}, \frac{1}{c} $ to be in arithmetic progression, implying that $a$, $b$, and $c$ are in harmonic progression.

Answer: $\boxed{A}$

The differential equation $\log \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = 2x - 5y$ is equivalent to $\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{2x - 5y} = e^{2x}e^{-5y}$.

Separating variables yields $e^{5y} dy = e^{2x} dx$. Integrating both sides gives $\frac{e^{5y}}{5} = \frac{e^{2x}}{2} + C$.

Applying the initial condition $y(0) = 0$ produces $\frac{1}{5} = \frac{1}{2} + C$, so $C = -\frac{3}{10}$.

Thus, $\frac{e^{5y}}{5} = \frac{e^{2x}}{2} - \frac{3}{10}$. Multiplying through by 10 and rearranging terms leads to $5e^{2x} - 2e^{5y} = 3$.

This matches option $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

62204.text: Let $I=\int \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{2 x}{1-x^2}\right) d x$, then $I-2 x \tan ^{-1} x=$
62204.sol:
Start with the integral $I = \int \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2x}{1 - x^2}\right) dx$. Using the identity $2 \tan^{-1} x = \tan^{-1} \left(\frac{2x}{1 - x^2}\right), valid for $-1 < x < 1$, rewrite the integral as $I = $\int2 \tan^{-1} x dx$.

Apply integration by parts, letting $u = \tan^{-1} x$ and $dv = 2 dx$, so $du = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}$ dx$ and $v = 2x$. This gives:

$I = 2x \tan^{-1} x - $\int \frac{2x}{1 + x^2}$ dx$

To evaluate the remaining integral, let $t = 1 + x²$ and $dt = 2x dx$, which yields:

\int \frac{2x}{1 + x^2}$ dx = $\int \frac{dt}{t} = \log |$ t| + C = $\log$(1 + x²) + C$

Substitute back to find:

$I = 2x $\tan^{-1} x$ - $\log$(1 + x²) + C$

The desired expression simplifies as:

$I - 2x $\tan^{-1} x$ = -$\log$(1 + x²) + C$

This corresponds to option B.

Answer: B

$

63606.subject: Mathematics
63606.text: An urn contains 6 yellow balls and $x$ black balls. When two balls are drawn at random, the probability that both are yellow is $\frac{5}{26}$, then the value of $x$ is
63606.sol:
Let $Y = 6$ be the number of yellow balls and $X = x$ be the number of black balls, so the total number of balls is $N = 6 + x$.

The probability of drawing two yellow balls is the ratio of combinations: $\frac{\binom{6}{2}}{\binom{6 + x}{2}} = \frac{5}{26}$.

Evaluating the combinations, $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ and $\binom{6 + x}{2} = \frac{(6 + x)(5 + x)}{2}$, so:

$\frac{15}{\frac{(6 + x)(5 + x)}{2}} = \frac{5}{26}$.

Simplifying, $\frac{30}{(6 + x)(5 + x)} = \frac{5}{26}$.

Dividing both sides by 5: $\frac{6}{(6 + x)(5 + x)} = \frac{1}{26}$.

Cross-multiplying: $(6 + x)(5 + x) = 156$.

Solving, $x^2 + 11x + 30 = 156$ and then $x^2 + 11x - 126 = 0$.

Factoring, $(x - 7)(x + 18) = 0$, so $x = 7$ (since $x \geq 0$).

The number of black balls is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

64494.subject: Mathematics
64494.text: If the lines $\frac{3-x}{2}=\frac{5 y-2}{3 \lambda+1}=5-z$ and $\frac{x+2}{-1}=\frac{1-3 y}{7}=\frac{4-z}{2 \mu}$ are at right angles, then $7 \lambda-10 \mu=$
64494.sol:
Transform the given line equations into symmetric form to extract direction ratios. For the first line, $\frac{3-x}{2} = \frac{5y-2}{3\lambda+1} = 5-z$, rewrite as:

$\frac{x-3}{-2} = \frac{y - \frac{2}{5}}{\frac{3\lambda+1}{5}} = \frac{z-5}{-1}$

The direction ratios are $d_1 = \langle -2, \frac{3\lambda+1}{5}, -1 \rangle$.

For the second line, $\frac{x+2}{-1} = \frac{1-3y}{7} = \frac{4-z}{2\mu}$, rewrite as:

$\frac{x+2}{-1} = \frac{y - \frac{1}{3}}{-\frac{7}{3}} = \frac{z-4}{-2\mu}$

The direction ratios are $d_2 = \langle -1, -\frac{7}{3}, -2\mu \rangle$.

Apply the perpendicularity condition $d_1 \cdot d_2 = 0$:

$(-2)(-1) + \left(\frac{3\lambda+1}{5}\right)\left(-\frac{7}{3}\right) + (-1)(-2\mu) = 0$
$2 - \frac{7(3\lambda+1)}{15} + 2\mu = 0$

Multiply the entire equation by 15 to eliminate denominators:

$30 - 7(3\lambda+1) + 30\mu = 0$
$30 - 21\lambda - 7 + 30\mu = 0$
$23 - 21\lambda + 30\mu = 0$

Rearrange to $21\lambda - 30\mu = 23$.

Compute the required expression $7\lambda - 10\mu$ by observing that it is one-third of the left-hand side:

$21\lambda - 30\mu = 3(7\lambda - 10\mu) = 23$

66532.text: When light of wavelength '$\lambda$' is incident on a photosensitive surface, the stopping potential is 'V'. When a light of wavelength $1.5\lambda$ is incident on the same surface, the stopping potential is '$\dfrac{V}{4}$'. Threshold wavelength for the surface is
66532.sol:
Using Einstein's photoelectric equation:

$eV = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}$

For the second case:

$e\left(\dfrac{V}{4}\right) = \dfrac{hc}{1.5\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}$

Multiplying the second equation by $4$ gives:

$eV = \dfrac{4hc}{1.5\lambda} - \dfrac{4hc}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{8hc}{3\lambda} - \dfrac{4hc}{\lambda_0}$

Equating the two expressions for $eV$:

$\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{8hc}{3\lambda} - \dfrac{4hc}{\lambda_0}$

Dividing by $hc$ and rearranging the terms:

$\dfrac{4}{\lambda_0} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{8}{3\lambda} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$

$\dfrac{3}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{5}{3\lambda}$

$\lambda_0 = \dfrac{9}{5}\lambda$

Answer: $\dfrac{9}{5}\lambda$

66540.text:
The ratio of the accelerating potentials required to accelerate (i) an $\alpha$-particle and (ii) a proton to have the same de Broglie wavelength associated with them is
(mass of $\alpha$ - particle = $6.4 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, mass of proton = $1.6 \times 10^{-27}$ kg)
66540.sol:
The de Broglie wavelength is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$.

Since the de Broglie wavelengths are the same, $\lambda_{\alpha} = \lambda_{p}$.

$\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}V_{\alpha}}} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{p}q_{p}V_{p}}}$

$m_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}V_{\alpha} = m_{p}q_{p}V_{p}$

$\dfrac{V_{\alpha}}{V_{p}} = \dfrac{m_{p}q_{p}}{m_{\alpha}q_{\alpha}}$

Given $m_{\alpha} = 6.4 \times 10^{-27}$ kg and $m_{p} = 1.6 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, we have $m_{\alpha} = 4m_{p}$.

The charge of an $\alpha$-particle is twice that of a proton, so $q_{\alpha} = 2q_{p}$.

$\dfrac{V_{\alpha}}{V_{p}} = \dfrac{m_{p} \times q_{p}}{4m_{p} \times 2q_{p}} = \dfrac{1}{8}$

The ratio is $1 : 8$.

Answer: $1 : 8$

Evaluating the options: Option A is incorrect due to mismatched frequency and intensity relations. Option B fails on $f_b > f_c$ and $I_c > I_d$. Option C correctly states $f_b < f_c$ and $I_c < I_d$ but errs with $f_b < f_a$. Option D is incorrect except for $f_b \leq f_a$. 66791.text: Two circuits $A$ and $B$ are connected to identical d.c. sources each of e.m.f. 10 volt. Self-inductances of circuits $A$ and $B$ are respectively $L_A=10 H$ and $L_B=10 \mathrm{mH}$. The total resistance of each circuit is $40 \Omega$. The ratio of energy consumed in circuit A and circuit B to build up the current to steady value is
66791.sol:
To determine the ratio of energy consumed in circuits A and B while building up the current to a steady value, the energy stored in the inductor at steady state is compared. The energy stored is given by $U = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$, where $L$ is the self-inductance and $I$ is the steady-state current.

The steady-state current is identical for both circuits due to the same emf of $10 \text{ V}$ and total resistance of $40 \Omega$, resulting in $I_0 = \frac{10}{40} = 0.25$ A.

Circuit A has $L_A = 10$ H, so the energy is $U_A = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10 \cdot (0.25)^2 = 0.3125$ J.

Circuit B has $L_B = 10$ mH = $0.01$ H, thus $U_B = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0.01 \cdot (0.25)^2 = 0.0003125$ J.

The ratio is $\frac{U_A}{U_B} = \frac{0.3125}{0.0003125} = 1000$.

The ratio is therefore 1000, symbolizing that the energy consumed in circuit A is a thousand times greater than in circuit B.

Answer: $1000$

69172.subject: Physics
69172.text: The relative angular speed of hour hand and minute hand of clock is
69172.sol:
The angular speed of the minute hand is the angle covered in one revolution divided by the time taken (1 hour = 3600 s):

$\omega_m = \dfrac{2\pi}{3600} = \dfrac{\pi}{1800}$ rad/s

The angular speed of the hour hand is the angle covered in one revolution divided by the time taken (12 hours = $12 \times 3600$ s = 43200 s):

$\omega_h = \dfrac{2\pi}{43200} = \dfrac{\pi}{21600}$ rad/s

The relative angular speed of the minute hand with respect to the hour hand is the difference between their angular speeds:

$\omega_{rel} = \omega_m - \omega_h$

$\omega_{rel} = \dfrac{\pi}{1800} - \dfrac{\pi}{21600}$

$\omega_{rel} = \dfrac{12\pi - \pi}{21600} = \dfrac{11\pi}{21600}$ rad/s

Answer: $\dfrac{11\pi}{21600}$

69954.text:
A polyatomic gas is compressed to $\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{\text{th }}$ of its volume adiabatically.
If its initial pressure is $P_0$, its new pressure will be $\left[\right.$ Given, $\left.\frac{C_p}{C_v}=4 / 3\right]$
69954.sol:
Adiabatic compression of a polyatomic gas follows $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$, with $\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = \frac{4}{3}$. The volume is compressed to $V_f = \frac{V_0}{8}$, where $V_0$ is the initial volume.

Using the relation $P_0 V_0^{\gamma} = P_f V_f^{\gamma}$ with the given values, solve for the final pressure:

$P_f = P_0 \frac{V_0^{\frac{4}{3}}}{\left(\frac{V_0}{8}\right)^{\frac{4}{3}}}$

Simplify the fraction:

$P_f = P_0 \times 8^{\frac{4}{3}}$

Evaluate the exponent: $8^{\frac{4}{3}} = (8^{\frac{1}{3}})^4 = 2^4 = 16$, so:

$P_f = P_0 \times 16 = 16 P_0$

Final pressure: $\boxed{\text{D}}$

70139.text: In a Fraunhofer diffraction of a single slit, when a slit is illuminated by a light of wavelength $6480\ \text{Å}$, angular width of central maximum is measured. When the slit is illuminated by light of another wavelength '$\lambda$' the angular width decreases by $25\%$. The value of $\lambda$ in $\text{Å}$ units is
70139.sol:
The angular width of the central maximum in a single slit Fraunhofer diffraction is given by $\theta = \dfrac{2\lambda}{a}$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of light and $a$ is the width of the slit.

From this relation, the angular width is directly proportional to the wavelength, $\theta \propto \lambda$.

Let the initial wavelength be $\lambda_1 = 6480\ \text{Å}$ with angular width $\theta_1$. When the angular width decreases by $25\%$, the new angular width becomes $\theta_2 = \theta_1 - 0.25\theta_1 = 0.75\theta_1$.

Since $\theta \propto \lambda$, the new wavelength $\lambda$ is given by $\lambda = 0.75\lambda_1$.

Substituting the given value of $\lambda_1$:

$\lambda = 0.75 \times 6480 = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 6480 = 4860\ \text{Å}$

70444.text: A sonometer wire resonates with $4$ antinodes between the two bridges for a given tuning fork when $1$ kg mass is suspended from the wire. Using same fork, when mass M is suspended, the wire resonates producing $2$ antinodes between the two bridges. (Distance between the bridges as before) The value of M is
70444.sol:
The frequency of a sonometer wire is given by $f = \dfrac{p}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$, where $p$ is the number of antinodes, $L$ is the length, $T$ is the tension, and $\mu$ is the linear mass density.

Since the frequency $f$, length $L$, and linear mass density $\mu$ are constant, we have $p \sqrt{T} = \text{constant}$.

Therefore, $p_1 \sqrt{T_1} = p_2 \sqrt{T_2}$.

Given $p_1 = 4$, $T_1 = 1 \times g$, $p_2 = 2$, and $T_2 = M \times g$.

Substituting the values, we get $4 \sqrt{1 \times g} = 2 \sqrt{M \times g}$.

Dividing by $2\sqrt{g}$, we get $2 = \sqrt{M}$.

Squaring both sides, $M = 4$ kg.

Answer: $4$ kg

71259.text: In their experiment to prove DNA replication is semi-conservative, Meselson and Stahl used 6M $\text{CsCl}$ because the density gradient value of 6M $\text{CsCl}$ is ________ the density gradient value of $^{15}\text{N}$ DNA.
71259.sol:
Meselson and Stahl used heavy isotope $^{15}\text{N}$ to label DNA and separated the heavy DNA from normal DNA using Cesium Chloride ($\text{CsCl}$) density gradient centrifugation.

The density of 6M $\text{CsCl}$ is approximately $1.7 \text{ g/cm}^3$, which is almost equal to the buoyant density of DNA.

During centrifugation, a density gradient is established, and DNA molecules move to the position in the gradient where the density of the $\text{CsCl}$ solution exactly matches their own density. Therefore, 6M $\text{CsCl}$ was chosen because its density gradient value is almost equal to the density gradient value of $^{15}\text{N}$ DNA.

Answer: almost equal to

72232.text: The pressure $P$, volume $V$ and temperature $T$ of a gas in the jar A and the other gas in the jar B is at pressure $2P$, volume $V/4$ and temperature $2T$, then the ratio of the number of molecules in the jar A and B will be
72232.sol:
Using the ideal gas equation, $PV = NkT$, where $N$ is the number of molecules.

For jar A:
$N_A = \dfrac{PV}{kT}$

For jar B:
$N_B = \dfrac{P_B V_B}{k T_B} = \dfrac{(2P)(V/4)}{k(2T)} = \dfrac{PV/2}{2kT} = \dfrac{PV}{4kT}$

Ratio of number of molecules:
$\dfrac{N_A}{N_B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{PV}{kT}}{\dfrac{PV}{4kT}} = \dfrac{4}{1}$

The ratio is $4 : 1$.

Answer: $4 : 1$

73789.subject: General Ability
73789.text:
The force-time $(F\text{-}t)$ graph of a $10\,\text{kg}$ moving object is shown below:

What is the final speed of the object?
73789.sol:
The area under the force-time ($F$-$t$) graph gives the impulse, which is equal to the change in momentum of the object.

$\text{Impulse} = \text{Area of the trapezium}$

$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (\text{sum of parallel sides}) \times \text{height}$

$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (25 + 15) \times 20$

$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 20 = 400 \, \text{N}\cdot\text{s}$

By the impulse-momentum theorem:

$\Delta p = m(v - u)$

Assuming the object starts from rest ($u = 0$):

$400 = 10 \times (v - 0)$

$v = 40 \, \text{m/s}$

Answer: $40\,\text{m/s}$

75141.text:
With reference to the territorial jurisdictions of High Courts in India, consider the following pairs:
High CourtsTerritorial Jurisdictions
I. Calcutta High CourtLakshadweep
II. Madras High CourtPuducherry
III. Gauhati High CourtManipur

How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
75141.sol:
The Calcutta High Court has territorial jurisdiction over West Bengal and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Lakshadweep comes under the jurisdiction of the Kerala High Court. Thus, Pair I is incorrectly matched.

The Madras High Court has territorial jurisdiction over Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. Thus, Pair II is correctly matched.

The Gauhati High Court has territorial jurisdiction over Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh. Manipur has its own High Court, established in $2013$. Thus, Pair III is incorrectly matched.

The Kerala High Court has territorial jurisdiction over Kerala and Lakshadweep. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands come under the jurisdiction of the Calcutta High Court. Thus, Pair IV is incorrectly matched.

Only one pair is correctly matched.

Answer: One

76478.text: For $x \geq y > 1$, let $\log _x\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)+\log _y\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)=k$, then the value of $k$ can never be equal to:

& \Rightarrow \quad 1-\log _x y+1-\frac{1}{\log _x y}=k \\
& \text{ Let, } \quad \log _x y=t \\
& \therefore \quad 2-t-\frac{1}{t}=k \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2 t-t^2-1=k t \\
& \Rightarrow \quad t^2+(k-2) t+1=0 \\
& \text{$ For $solution, } \quad \mathrm{D}=b^2-4 a c \geq 0 \\
& (k-2)^2-4 \geq 0 \quad(k-2)^2 \geq 0 \\
& k-2 \geq 2 \quad k-2 \leq 0 \\
& k \geq 4 \quad k \leq 0 \\
& \therefore k \geq 4 \text{ or } k \leq 0
\end{aligned}$

77470.text:
For the following two (02) items:
Let $u = \int e^x \cos x\, dx$ and $v = \int e^x \sin x\, dx$.

Consider the following:
I. $\dfrac{du}{dx} = -v$
II. $\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -u$
Which of the above is/are correct?
77470.sol:
Given $u = \int e^x \cos x\, dx$ and $v = \int e^x \sin x\, dx$.

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$, we get:
$\dfrac{du}{dx} = e^x \cos x$
$\dfrac{dv}{dx} = e^x \sin x$

Evaluating the integrals, we have:
$u = \dfrac{e^x}{2}(\cos x + \sin x) + C_1$
$v = \dfrac{e^x}{2}(\sin x - \cos x) + C_2$

Comparing the derivatives with $u$ and $v$, it is clear that:
$\dfrac{du}{dx} \neq -v$
$\dfrac{dv}{dx} \neq -u$

Therefore, neither statement I nor statement II is correct.

82481.subject: Physics
82481.text:
A photon and an electron, each of $20$ eV energy, move in free space. The ratio of linear momentum of electron $p_e$ to that of photon $p_{Ph}$, $\dfrac{p_e}{p_{Ph}}$ is :
(Take speed of light $=3\times10^8$ ms$^{-1}$, charge of electron $=-1.6\times10^{-19}$ C and mass of electron $=9\times10^{-31}$ kg)
82481.sol:
For a photon, the energy $E$ and linear momentum $p_{Ph}$ are related by:

$p_{Ph} = \dfrac{E}{c}$

For an electron, the kinetic energy $E$ and linear momentum $p_e$ are related by:

$p_e = \sqrt{2mE}$

The ratio of the linear momentum of the electron to that of the photon is:

$\dfrac{p_e}{p_{Ph}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\dfrac{E}{c}} = c \sqrt{\dfrac{2m}{E}}$

Given:
$E = 20 \text{ eV} = 20 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 32 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$
$m = 9 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$
$c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$

Substituting the values into the ratio:

$\dfrac{p_e}{p_{Ph}} = 3 \times 10^8 \times \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^{-31}}{32 \times 10^{-19}}}$

$\dfrac{p_e}{p_{Ph}} = 3 \times 10^8 \times \sqrt{\dfrac{18 \times 10^{-31}}{32 \times 10^{-19}}}$

$\dfrac{p_e}{p_{Ph}} = 3 \times 10^8 \times \sqrt{\dfrac{9}{16} \times 10^{-12}}$

$\dfrac{p_e}{p_{Ph}} = 3 \times 10^8 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{4} \times 10^{-6}\right)$

$\dfrac{p_e}{p_{Ph}} = \dfrac{9}{4} \times 10^2 = 2.25 \times 100 = 225$

83202.subject: Physics
83202.text: The half life of a radioactive substance is$20$minutes. In how much time, the activity of substance drops to $\left(\dfrac{1}{16}\right)th$ of its initial value?
83202.sol:
Activity of substance is given by, $A = \dfrac{{A}_{0}}{{2}^{n}}$, where $n$ is the number of half-lives.

Now, $\dfrac{{A}_{0}}{16} = \dfrac{{A}_{0}}{{2}^{n}} ⇒ n = 4$

Therefore,

$n = \dfrac{t}{{T}_{\dfrac{1}{2}}} ⇒ t = 4T\dfrac{1}{2} = 4 \times 20min = 80min$

83406.subject: Physics
83406.text: A solid sphere $A$ of radius $R$ and mass $M$ is attached at a point to a smaller solid sphere $B$ of radius $r < R$ and mass $m < M$. Assume that the line joining their centres lies along the horizontal. The moment of inertia of the system calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of $A$ is $I_A$ and that calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of $B$ is $I_B$. The difference $I_A-I_B$ is :
83406.sol:
The distance between the centres of the two spheres $A$ and $B$ is $d = R + r$.

Let $I_{A,\text{cm}}$ and $I_{B,\text{cm}}$ be the moments of inertia of spheres $A$ and $B$ about their respective vertical centroidal axes. For solid spheres, $I_{A,\text{cm}} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$ and $I_{B,\text{cm}} = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$.

The moment of inertia of the system about a vertical axis passing through the centre of $A$ is given by the sum of the moment of inertia of $A$ about its own centre and the moment of inertia of $B$ about the centre of $A$. Using the parallel axis theorem:
$I_A = I_{A,\text{cm}} + \left[ I_{B,\text{cm}} + m(R+r)^2 \right]$

Similarly, the moment of inertia of the system about a vertical axis passing through the centre of $B$ is:
$I_B = \left[ I_{A,\text{cm}} + M(R+r)^2 \right] + I_{B,\text{cm}}$

Now, finding the difference $I_A - I_B$:
$I_A - I_B = \left( I_{A,\text{cm}} + I_{B,\text{cm}} + m(R+r)^2 \right) - \left( I_{A,\text{cm}} + M(R+r)^2 + I_{B,\text{cm}} \right)$

$I_A - I_B = m(R+r)^2 - M(R+r)^2$

$I_A - I_B = (m - M)(R+r)^2$

Answer: $(m-M)(R+r)^2$

87863.text: Geometrical shapes of the complexes formed by the reaction of ${Ni}^{2 +}withCl^{-}, CN^{-}and{H}_{2}O$ , respectively, are
87863.sol:
$Ni^{2 +} + 4CN^{-} \to {\left[Ni{\left(CN\right)}_{4}\right]}^{2 -}$

Here $Ni^{2 +}$ has $d^{8}$ -configuration with $CN^{-}$ as strong ligand.



$d^{8}$ -configuration in strong ligand field gives ${\text{dsp}^{2}$ hybridisation, hence square planar geometry.
$Ni^{2 +} + 4Cl^{-} \to {\left[NiC{l}_{4}\right]}^{2 -}$
Here $Ni^{2 +}$ has $d^{8}$ -configuration with $Cl^{-}$ as weak ligand.



$d^{8}$-configuration in weak ligand field gives $sp^{3}$hybridisation, hence tetrahedral geometry.
$Ni^{2 +}$ with ${H}_{2}O$ forms ${\left[Ni{\left({H}_{2}O\right)}_{6}\right]}^{2 +}$ complex and ${H}_{2}O$ is a weak ligand.



Therefore, ${\left[Ni{\left({H}_{2}O\right)}_{6}\right]}^{2 +}$ has octahedral geometry.
In octahedral complexes with $d^{8}$ configuration, there is always ${\text{sp}^{3} d^{2}$ hybridisation (outer orbital complex) irrespective of strong ligand field or weak ligand field.

89938.text: If $n$ is an even positive integer greater than $1 and x > 0$, then the condition that the greatest term in the expansion of $\left(1 + x\right)n$ may have the greatest coefficient also is
89938.sol:
If $n$ is even, the greatest coefficient is ${}^{n}{C}_{n / 2}$

$∴$ The greatest term $= {}^{n}{C}_{n / 2}x^{n / 2}$

$∴ {}^{n}{C}_{n / 2}x^{n / 2} > {}^{n}{C}_{\left(n / 2\right) - 1}x^{\left(n / 2\right) - 1}$

and ${}^{n}{C}_{n / 2}x^{n / 2} > {}^{n}{C}_{\left(n / 2\right) + 1}x^{\left(n / 2\right) + 1}$

$⇒\dfrac{n - \dfrac{n}{2} + 1}{n2}x > 1$

and $\dfrac{n - \left(\dfrac{n}{2} + 1\right) + 1}{\dfrac{n}{2} + 1}x < 1$

$⇒ \left(n / 2\right)\left(n / 2\right) + 1 < \text{x} < \left(\dfrac{n}{2} + 1\right)\dfrac{n}{2}$

Hence, $\dfrac{n}{n + 2} < x < \dfrac{n + 2}{n}$

93255.text: ${g}_{e}$ and ${g}_{p}$ denote the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the earth and another planet whose mass and radius are twice that of the earth, then
93255.sol:
Acceleration due to gravity is given by,

$g = \dfrac{GM}{R2}$

where $G$ is gravitational constant.

$Forearth: {g}_{e} = {GM}_{e}{R}_e^{2}$

$Forplanet: {g}_{p} = {GM}_{p}{R}_p^{2}$

$or\dfrac{ge}{gp} = \dfrac{Me}{Mp} \times {R}_p^{2}{R}_e^{2} \ldots \left(i\right)$

$Given, {M}_{p} = 2{M}_{e}, {R}_{p} = 2{R}_{e}$

Putting the values in the Eq. (i), we obtain

$\dfrac{ge}{gp} = \dfrac{Me}{2{M}_{e}} \times \left(2{R}_{e}\right)^{2}{R}_e^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{4}{1} =2$

$∴ {g}_{p} = \dfrac{ge}{2}$

95818.subject: Botany
95818.text: All eukaryotic unicellular organisms belong to the kingdom
95818.sol:
Kingdom Protista includes all single-celled eukaryotes. Protozoans, euglenoids, dinoflagellates are included in this group. Organisms in the kingdom are primarily aquatic and some show the presence of flagella and cilia.

All the chlorophyll-containing eukaryotes are included in the kingdom Plantae. All the organisms in it have cell wall made of cellulose and are autotrophic (some partial autotrophic- insectivorous plant).

Kingdom Monera includes all the prokaryotic organisms including the autotrophic and heterotrophic groups. These have non-cellulosic cell wall like Fungi but it contains varying concentration of peptidoglycan. All bacteria are included in this kingdom.

Fungi form a unique group of heterotrophic organisms showing wide diversity. These organisms have cell wall which is made of chitin unlike cellulose seen in plants. The commonly consumed mushroom and toadstool are included in this kingdom. These organisms are achlorophyllous as they are all non-photosynthetic.

Kingdom Animalia includes all the multicellular-eukaryotic animals. The organisms are heterotrophic and lack cell walls. Animals digest their food internally showing holozoic nutrition. Majority of them show capacity of locomotion.

100127.subject: Physics
100127.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Pressure and energy density have the same dimensional formula.
Reason (R): Energy density is defined as the force acting per unit area.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
100127.sol:
Assertion (A) is true: The dimensional formula of pressure is $P = \dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Area}} = \dfrac{[\text{MLT}^{-2}]}{[\text{L}^2]} = [\text{ML}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}]$.
Energy density is energy per unit volume, so its dimensional formula is $u = \dfrac{\text{Energy}}{\text{Volume}} = \dfrac{[\text{ML}^2\text{T}^{-2}]}{[\text{L}^3]} = [\text{ML}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}]$.
Thus, pressure and energy density have the same dimensional formula.

Reason (R) is false: Energy density is defined as the energy stored per unit volume, not as force acting per unit area (which is the definition of pressure). Although they are dimensionally equivalent, their physical definitions are entirely different.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

\(v_y=u_y+a_y t=0+(10)(1)=10 $\mathrm{~m}$/ $\mathrm{s} .$\)
This matches (q) 10 SI unit.
- Note: Both A and B have the same value, which is common in physics problems.
C) Horizontal displacement:
Horizontal displacement is calculated using constant velocity.
\(x=u_x t=(10)(1)=10 $\mathrm{~m} .$\)
This matches (q) 10 SI unit.
- Note: A, B, and C all have the same value. This confirms our calculations.
D) Vertical displacement:
Vertical displacement is calculated using constant acceleration.
\(y=u_y t+$\frac{1}{2}$a_y t²=(0)(1)+$\frac{1}{2}($10)(1)^2=0+5=5 $\mathrm{~m} .$\)
This matches (p) 5 SI unit.
Final Matches
- \($\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{q}$\)
- \($\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{q}$\)
- \($\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{q}$\)
- \($\mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}$\)

102434.subject: Physics
102434.text: A particle is executing simple harmonic motion with an amplitude $A$. What is the phase difference between its velocity and acceleration at the instant when its displacement is $x = \dfrac{A}{2}$?
102434.sol:
In simple harmonic motion, the equations for displacement, velocity, and acceleration can be written as:

$x = A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$

$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = A\omega \cos(\omega t + \phi) = A\omega \sin\left(\omega t + \phi + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -A\omega^2 \sin(\omega t + \phi) = A\omega^2 \sin(\omega t + \phi + \pi)$

The phase of the velocity is $\left(\omega t + \phi + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and the phase of the acceleration is $(\omega t + \phi + \pi)$.

The phase difference between velocity and acceleration is:
$\Delta\Phi = (\omega t + \phi + \pi) - \left(\omega t + \phi + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ radians}$

This phase difference is a constant value that depends only on the mathematical relationship between the kinematic variables. It is entirely independent of the particle's instantaneous position or time.

Therefore, even at the specific position $x = \dfrac{A}{2}$ (where the phase angle of displacement happens to be $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$), the phase difference between velocity and acceleration remains exactly $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}$

106458.subject: Chemistry
106458.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The plot of radial wavefunction ($\psi$) versus distance ($r$) for a $2p$ orbital starts from a non-zero value and crosses the $r$-axis exactly once.
Reason (R): For a $2p$ orbital, the number of radial nodes is zero, and $s$-orbitals are the only orbitals where the radial wavefunction is non-zero at the nucleus.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is incorrect
Assertion (A) is incorrect but Reason (R) is correct
106458.sol:
Assertion (A) is incorrect. For a $2p$ orbital, the principal quantum number $n = 2$ and the azimuthal quantum number $l = 1$. The number of radial nodes is given by $n - l - 1 = 2 - 1 - 1 = 0$. Therefore, its $\psi$ versus $r$ plot does not cross the $r$-axis. Furthermore, since it is a p-orbital ($l = 1$), the radial wavefunction is zero at the nucleus ($r = 0$), so the plot must start from the origin.

Reason (R) is correct. The calculation $n - l - 1 = 0$ confirms that a $2p$ orbital has zero radial nodes. According to quantum mechanics, only $s$-orbitals ($l = 0$) have a non-zero probability amplitude (wavefunction) at the nucleus. For all other orbitals ($p, d, f, \dots$), the wavefunction is zero at the nucleus.

Answer: Assertion (A) is incorrect but Reason (R) is correct

106460.subject: Chemistry
106460.text: The maximum numerical value of the magnetic quantum number ($m_l$) observed for an electron in an atom's ground state is $+2$. What is the minimum possible value of the principal quantum number ($n$) for this electron, and what is the total number of orbitals present in that principal shell?
106460.sol:
The magnetic quantum number $m_l$ can take integral values from $-l$ to $+l$, including zero. If the maximum observed value of $m_l$ is $+2$, the azimuthal quantum number $l$ must be at least $2$ (which corresponds to a d-subshell).

The principal quantum number $n$ must be strictly greater than $l$ ($n > l$). Therefore, the minimum possible value for $n$ is $2 + 1 = 3$.

For a principal shell with quantum number $n$, the total number of orbitals is given by the formula $n^2$. For $n = 3$, the total number of orbitals is $3^2 = 9$.

Note: $5$ is the number of orbitals in the d-subshell alone, and $18$ is the maximum number of electrons in the $n=3$ shell, not the number of orbitals.

Answer: $n = 3$, total orbitals = $9$

Therefore, Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

114398.subject: Chemistry
114398.text:
A galvanic cell consists of a standard zinc half-cell and a hydrogen half-cell. The cell is represented as:

$\text{Zn(s)} \mid \text{Zn}^{2+}(0.1\text{ M}) \parallel \text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) \mid \text{H}_{2}(1\text{ bar}) \mid \text{Pt}$

If the measured emf of the cell is $0.642\text{ V}$ at $298\text{ K}$, what is the pH of the solution in the hydrogen half-cell?
(Given: $E^{\circ}_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}$ and $\dfrac{2.303\text{ RT}}{\text{F}} = 0.059\text{ V}$ at $298\text{ K}$)
114398.sol:
The cell reaction is:
$\text{Zn(s)} + 2\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{H}_{2}(\text{g})$

The standard cell potential is:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0.00 - (-0.76) = 0.76\text{ V}$

The number of electrons transferred, $n = 2$.

Using the Nernst equation:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]P_{\text{H}_{2}}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}}$

Substitute the given values:
$0.642 = 0.76 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{0.1 \times 1}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}}$

$0.642 = 0.76 - 0.0295 \log \dfrac{10^{-1}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^{2}}$

$0.76 - 0.642 = 0.0295 (\log 10^{-1} - \log [\text{H}^{+}]^{2})$

$0.118 = 0.0295 (-1 - 2\log [\text{H}^{+}])$

Since $\text{pH} = -\log [\text{H}^{+}]$, we can write $-2\log [\text{H}^{+}] = 2\text{pH}$:
$0.118 = 0.0295 (-1 + 2\text{pH})$

$\dfrac{0.118}{0.0295} = -1 + 2\text{pH}$

$4 = -1 + 2\text{pH}$

$2\text{pH} = 5 \Rightarrow \text{pH} = 2.5$

Forgetting to square the $[\text{H}^{+}]$ term leads to an incorrect pH of $5.0$, while using $n=1$ leads to $1.5$.

Answer: $2.5$

118253.subject: Chemistry
118253.text:
An unknown alkene 'X' undergoes the following sequence of reactions to yield 3-methylbu\tan^{-1}-amine as the major final product:
(i) $\text{HBr}$, benzoyl peroxide
(ii) $\text{KCN}$
(iii) $\text{Na(Hg)} / \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$

The IUPAC name of the starting alkene 'X' is:
118253.sol:
The problem can be solved by retrosynthetic analysis.

The final product is 3-methylbu\tan^{-1}-amine ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$). This is formed by the reduction of a nitrile in step (iii). Therefore, the precursor nitrile must be 3-methylbutanenitrile ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CN}$).

The nitrile is formed in step (ii) by the nucleophilic substitution of an alkyl bromide with $\text{KCN}$. Thus, the alkyl bromide must be 1-bromo-2-methylpropane ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$).

In step (i), 1-bromo-2-methylpropane is formed by the anti-Markovnikov addition of $\text{HBr}$ in the presence of peroxide to an alkene. The only alkene that yields this specific primary bromide under these conditions is 2-methylpropene ($\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{CH}_2$).

Using but-1-ene would yield pen\tan^{-1}-amine, while but-2-ene would yield 2-methylbu\tan^{-1}-amine.

Answer: 2-Methylpropene

121007.subject: Chemistry
121007.text:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Prosthetic group(I) Transient association with apoenzyme
(B) Co-enzyme(II) Tightly bound organic compound
(C) Metal ion(III) Zinc in carboxypeptidase
(D) Apoenzyme(IV) Protein portion of the enzyme

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
121007.sol:
Based on the classification of cofactors in enzymes:

(A) Prosthetic groups are organic compounds that are distinguished from other cofactors in that they are tightly bound to the apoenzyme. Hence, (A) matches with (II).

(B) Co-enzymes are also organic compounds but their association with the apoenzyme is only transient, usually occurring during the course of catalysis. Hence, (B) matches with (I).

(C) Metal ions form coordination bonds with side chains at the active site and at the same time form one or more coordination bonds with the substrate. Zinc is a metal ion cofactor for the proteolytic enzyme carboxypeptidase. Hence, (C) matches with (III).

(D) The protein portion of the enzyme is called the apoenzyme. Hence, (D) matches with (IV).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
